title: Mara's army
hookLine: Mara comes with storms and armies, then his daughters; the arrows fall as flowers

lines: EVERYTHING THAT WANTS YOU TO LEAVE.
cards: You sit down to be quiet for two minutes, and the attack begins. Not from outside. From inside.
The email you forgot to send. The thing someone said last week. Your knee.
A sudden craving for something sweet. A voice that says this is pointless, who do you think you are. The moment you decide to stay, everything that wants you to leave can seem to show up at once.
Under the tree, the wanderer has made his vow. And the old tellings say that the moment he did, someone noticed. Someone who had been waiting since the palace gate.

teach.b: Mara. The name comes from the same root as marana, death. Mara is the one who kills, or the one who keeps you in the cycle of death and rebirth.
Buddhists speak of him as a god-like tempter, and also as a picture of everything in the mind that resists waking up. The later telling makes the attack enormous.
Mara rides out on a giant elephant with an army stretching to the horizon, every soldier armed. He sends storms: wind, then rain, rocks, weapons, burning coals, hot ash, sand, mud, and darkness.
And everything he throws turns into flowers and perfume, drifting down around the seated man like offerings.
In some tellings, Mara's three daughters come too, beautiful, to tempt him. In a sutta, they arrive after the awakening instead, and fail just the same.

But in a poem in the Sutta Nipata, in the Pali canon, the Buddha names Mara's army himself, and its soldiers live closer to home. Your first army, he tells Mara, is sensual desire. The second, discontent.
The third, hunger and thirst. The fourth, craving. The fifth, sloth and drowsiness.
The sixth, fear. The seventh, doubt. The eighth, hypocrisy and stubbornness.
The ninth, gain and fame and honor wrongly won. The tenth, praising yourself and looking down on others.
Not demons on elephants. Discontent, fear, doubt, the need to be seen. In the poem, he doesn't run; he says he will break this army with wisdom, the way a stone breaks an unbaked clay pot.
In the later telling, he doesn't even move. He stays on the seat, and everything thrown at him falls like petals.

how: Buddhist temple murals show Mara's army and the weapons turning to flowers, and some meditation teachers speak of noticing 'Mara' in the mind's own distractions, naming them without obeying them.

o: a demon king who guards the Bodhi tree
a mountain spirit who guards the Himalayas
the tempter, whose name comes from death

games.q: what's inside Mara's army — tap the pairs.

s: in every telling, Mara's daughters come during the night under the tree
in SN 4.25 they come after the awakening; some later tellings put them in the night.
the Sutta Nipata names fear and doubt among Mara's armies
the sixth is fear, the seventh doubt.
in the later telling, he hurled Mara's weapons back at the army
he stayed on the seat, and the weapons fell as flowers.

games.q: you're on your seat, and an army hurls rocks, weapons and burning coals at you. what do you do?
games.why: he stays. in the telling, everything thrown turns to flowers and perfume and drifts down around him.

practice: As you sit, watch for Mara's army, and when something arrives to pull you off the seat, name it softly: wanting, doubt, boredom, fear, drowsiness.
Don't fight it and don't obey it; picture it landing near you like a petal, let it lie there, and come back to the breath. The next one will come; name it too.

wordCard.voice: Mara. The tempter, whose name comes from death, who attacked the wanderer with storms and armies that fell as flowers.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: the tempter, the one who kills; from the root mṛ, to die.

carryVoice: Your line: the arrows become flowers. The night isn't over yet. Day fifty-two is yours.
